about: The scripted AI lesson for p1-efficiency (2026-11-17, Phase B, brief docs/briefs/2026-11-15-script-four-topics.md): every word she sees is written here once and checked (tools/check-script.js, tools/review-lesson.js --script). The AI only marks her typed answers (choosing a branch written here), answers her own questions, and sorts her messages. It opens with two recall questions from p1-energy-stores and p1-conservation.

steps.text: Welcome! This lesson is about efficiency: how much of the energy put into a machine does the job you want, how to work it out, and how to make machines better at it.

steps.question: First, two quick questions from earlier lessons. Where does the energy a machine wastes usually end up?

options.text: In the thermal store of the surroundings

steps.right: Yes: it is dissipated into the thermal store of the surroundings.

wrong.other: Not quite: in the thermal store of the surroundings.
wrong.destroyed: Not quite: energy is never destroyed. The energy a machine wastes is dissipated into the thermal store of the surroundings.
wrong.battery: Not quite: it does not go back. The energy a machine wastes is dissipated into the thermal store of the surroundings.

idk.hint: The energy a machine wastes warms the air around it a tiny bit. Which button fits?

steps.answerWhy: The energy a machine wastes is dissipated into the thermal store of the surroundings.

steps.question: Second: oil is put between the moving parts of a machine. What does it reduce?
steps.right: Yes: oil reduces friction, so less energy is wasted by heating the parts.

wrong.other: Not quite: friction. Oil lets the parts slide more easily.
wrong.air: Not quite: friction. Air resistance is the push of the air; oil works between parts that rub.
wrong.supply: Not quite: friction. Oil does not change what is supplied; it lets the parts slide more easily, so less is wasted.

idk.hint: Oil helps parts slide over each other. Which force tries to stop surfaces sliding?

steps.answerWhy: Oil reduces friction, so less energy is wasted by heating the parts.

steps.text: Now this lesson. A lamp is supplied with 100 J and gives out 20 J as light. The other 80 J warms the lamp and the air around it, and is wasted.
The energy that does the job you want is called the useful output energy transfer. For the lamp it is the 20 J of light.
All the energy supplied to a device is called the total input energy transfer: the useful part and the wasted part added together. For the lamp it is 100 J.

Efficiency is the proportion of the energy supplied that is transferred usefully. The equation is: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer. For the lamp, 20 ÷ 100 = 0.2.
Efficiency has no unit, because it is joules divided by joules. To give it as a percentage, multiply by 100: the lamp's 0.2 is 20%.

steps.question: A machine has an efficiency of 0.75. What does that mean?

options.text: 75% of the energy supplied is transferred usefully
It wastes 75% of the energy supplied

steps.right: Yes: 0.75 is 75%, so 75% of the energy supplied is transferred usefully, and the other 25% is wasted.

wrong.other: Not quite. 0.75 means 75% of the energy supplied is transferred usefully.
wrong.waste: Not quite: the other way round. Efficiency is the useful part, so 75% is transferred usefully and 25% is wasted.
wrong.joule: Not quite: efficiency has no unit. 0.75 is 75%, so 75% of the energy supplied is transferred usefully.

idk.hint: Multiply 0.75 by 100 to make it a percentage. Is efficiency the useful part or the wasted part?

steps.answerWhy: 0.75 is 75%, so 75% of the energy supplied is transferred usefully.

steps.question: Which of these efficiencies is impossible?
steps.right: Yes: 1.2 would mean more useful energy out than energy in. Energy cannot be created, so efficiency is never more than 1 (100%).

wrong.other: Not quite: 1.2. Efficiency can never be more than 1 (100%), because energy cannot be created.
wrong.high: Not quite: 0.95 is very good, but possible. 1.2 is impossible: it would mean more useful energy out than energy in.
wrong.low: Not quite: 0.05 is very poor, but possible. 1.2 is impossible: it would mean more useful energy out than energy in.

idk.hint: Can a machine give out more useful energy than it is given? Which number would mean that?

steps.answerWhy: Energy cannot be created, so efficiency is never more than 1 (100%): 1.2 is impossible.

steps.prompt: In one line: what is efficiency, and what is the highest it could ever be?
points: useful output energy divided by total input energy
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: efficiency is the useful output energy divided by the total input energy, and it can never be more than 1, or 100%.

steps.text: Here is a worked example. Tap "Show the first step" under it to see each step in turn.
steps.question: A motor is supplied with 500 J. It transfers 375 J usefully to a kinetic store. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?
steps: Write the equation: efficiency = useful output energy transfer ÷ total input energy transfer.

steps.question: Your turn. A speaker is supplied with 80 J and gives out 4 J as sound. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?

wrong.decimal: Nearly: 0.05 is the efficiency as a decimal. As a percentage, multiply by 100: 5%.
wrong.upside: Not quite: 5%. Put the useful energy on top: 4 ÷ 80 = 0.05, which is 5%. Over 100% always means it was divided the wrong way round.

idk.hint: Divide the useful energy, 4, by the total, 80. Then multiply by 100.

steps.text: Efficiency works with power too. Power is the energy transferred each second, in watts (W). Divide the useful power output by the total power input, just as with energy.

steps.question: A lamp is supplied with 10 W, and 9 W of that comes out as light. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?

wrong.decimal: Nearly: 0.9 is the efficiency as a decimal. As a percentage, multiply by 100: 90%.
wrong.upside: Not quite: 90%. Put the useful power on top: 9 ÷ 10 = 0.9, which is 90%.

idk.hint: Divide the useful power, 9, by the total power, 10. Then multiply by 100.

steps.text: Sometimes you know the efficiency and need an energy. Put the numbers into the equation first, then rearrange. For example, 0.4 = useful ÷ 200 gives useful = 0.4 × 200 = 80 J.

steps.question: A motor has an efficiency of 0.6. It is supplied with 500 J. How much energy does it transfer usefully, in joules?
steps.right: Yes: 300 J. 0.6 = useful ÷ 500, so useful = 0.6 × 500 = 300 J.

wrong.other: Not quite: 300 J. 0.6 = useful ÷ 500, so useful = 0.6 × 500 = 300 J.
wrong.divide: Not quite: 300 J. The useful energy cannot be more than the 500 J supplied. Multiply: useful = 0.6 × 500 = 300 J.

idk.hint: Put the numbers in: 0.6 = useful ÷ 500. Multiply both sides by 500.

steps.text: To use a percentage in the equation, change it back to a decimal first by dividing by 100. 80% is 0.8.

steps.question: A heater is 80% efficient and transfers 400 J usefully. What is the total input energy, in joules?

wrong.other: Not quite: 500 J. 0.8 = 400 ÷ total, so total = 400 ÷ 0.8 = 500 J.
wrong.times: Not quite: 500 J. The total input must be bigger than the useful 400 J. 0.8 = 400 ÷ total, so total = 400 ÷ 0.8 = 500 J.
wrong.percent: Not quite: 500 J. Change 80% to 0.8 first. Then total = 400 ÷ 0.8 = 500 J.

idk.hint: Change 80% to 0.8. Then put the numbers in: 0.8 = 400 ÷ total. Swap the total and the 0.8.

steps.prompt: In one line: how do you find the useful output energy if you know the efficiency and the total input energy?
points: multiply the efficiency (as a decimal) by the total input energy
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: multiply the efficiency, as a decimal, by the total input energy.

steps.text: To compare two devices, work out the efficiency of each one. The one with the higher efficiency wastes less of the energy it is given.
Old-style bulbs are called incandescent bulbs: a thin wire inside glows white hot. Most of their energy heats the room instead of making light.
Modern bulbs are called LEDs, short for light-emitting diodes. Given the same energy, an LED gives out much more light, so LEDs are more efficient.

steps.question: Motor A takes in 200 W and gives out 150 W usefully. Motor B takes in 500 W and gives out 300 W usefully. Which is more efficient?

options.text: Motor B: it gives out more useful power

steps.right: Yes: A is 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75, and B is 300 ÷ 500 = 0.6. A wastes a smaller share of its input.

wrong.other: Not quite: motor A. A is 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75 and B is 300 ÷ 500 = 0.6.
wrong.bigger: Not quite: B gives out more, but it also takes in much more. A is 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75, and B is 300 ÷ 500 = 0.6, so A is more efficient.
wrong.same: Not quite: work each one out. A is 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75, and B is 300 ÷ 500 = 0.6, so A is more efficient.

idk.hint: Work out each efficiency: 150 ÷ 200, then 300 ÷ 500. Which is bigger?

steps.answerWhy: A is 150 ÷ 200 = 0.75 and B is 300 ÷ 500 = 0.6, so motor A is more efficient.

steps.question: Why is a petrol car engine much less efficient than an electric motor?

options.text: Most of the energy from the fuel is wasted heating the engine and exhaust
Petrol has no energy in it
A petrol engine destroys some energy

steps.right: Yes: a petrol engine gets very hot, and most of the fuel's energy goes to heating the engine, the exhaust and the air.

wrong.other: Not quite. Most of the energy from the fuel is wasted heating the engine and exhaust.
wrong.noenergy: Not quite: petrol has lots of energy in its chemical store. Most of it is wasted heating the engine and exhaust.
wrong.destroys: Not quite: no machine destroys energy. Most of the fuel's energy is wasted heating the engine and exhaust.

idk.hint: A petrol engine gets very hot when it runs. What does that tell you about where its energy goes?

steps.answerWhy: Most of the fuel's energy is wasted heating the engine, the exhaust and the air.

steps.prompt: In one line: how do you decide which of two devices is more efficient?
points: work out the efficiency of each
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: work out the efficiency of each device; the one with the higher efficiency wastes less energy.

steps.text: Lubrication means putting oil between moving parts. It reduces friction, so less energy is wasted by heating, and the machine becomes more efficient.
Insulating hot parts, like a boiler, means less energy escapes to the surroundings. Swapping in better parts, like LEDs for incandescent bulbs, helps too.
A more efficient device needs less energy put in for the same useful output. Less input means less fuel burned in power stations, and lower electricity bills.

steps.question: An exam asks why a family should buy an efficient fridge. Which answer would score the marks?

options.text: It wastes less energy, so it needs less input, so bills are lower
It wastes no energy at all

steps.right: Yes: say what is wasted, what that means for the input, and what that means for the bill. Each link earns a mark.

wrong.other: Not quite. The answer that scores is: it wastes less energy, so it needs less input, so bills are lower.
wrong.saves: Not quite: "saves energy" scores nothing on its own. Say: it wastes less energy, so it needs less input energy, so the electricity bills are lower.
wrong.none: Not quite: every real device wastes some energy, so "wastes no energy" is marked wrong. It wastes less, so it needs less input, so bills are lower.

idk.hint: The best answer links three things: waste, input and bills. Which button links all three?

steps.answerWhy: An efficient fridge wastes less energy, so it needs less input energy, so the electricity bills are lower.

steps.prompt: In one line: give one way to make a machine more efficient, and say why it works.
points: a way: lubrication, insulation or better parts
steps.idk: No problem. A good line would be: lubricate the moving parts, which reduces friction, so less energy is wasted by heating.

steps.text: Now for a short quiz: six questions on the whole lesson. Take your time.

steps.question: Quiz, question 1 of 6: a device takes in 200 J and transfers 150 J usefully. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?
Quiz, question 2 of 6: what unit does efficiency have?
steps.right: Yes: none. It is joules divided by joules (or watts by watts).

wrong.other: Not quite: none. Efficiency is joules divided by joules (or watts by watts), so the units cancel.

steps.answerWhy: Efficiency has no unit: it is joules divided by joules.

steps.question: Quiz, question 3 of 6: a heater has a total power input of 50 W and a useful power output of 20 W. What is its efficiency, as a percentage?
Quiz, question 4 of 6: a motor has an efficiency of 0.25 and is supplied with 800 J. How much energy does it transfer usefully, in joules?

wrong.other: Not quite: 200 J. 0.25 = useful ÷ 800, so useful = 0.25 × 800 = 200 J.

steps.question: Quiz, question 5 of 6: which kind of bulb is more efficient at making light?
steps.right: Yes: an LED gives out more light from the same energy.

wrong.other: Not quite: an LED. Incandescent bulbs waste most of their energy heating the room.

steps.answerWhy: An LED gives out more light from the same energy, so it is more efficient.

steps.question: Quiz, question 6 of 6: someone gets an efficiency of 1.6. What did they most likely do?

options.text: Divided the total input by the useful output
Nothing: the machine is just very good

steps.right: Yes: dividing the wrong way round gives an answer over 1. Put the useful output on top.

wrong.other: Not quite: efficiency over 1 is impossible, so they divided the wrong way round. Put the useful output on top.

steps.answerWhy: An answer over 1 means the division was the wrong way round: useful output goes on top.
